description: Interpret break-even graphs, use the formula, and understand why cash matters.
content_html:
What Is Break-Even?

Every start-up needs to know how many units it must sell before it stops making a loss. The total revenue exactly equals total costs; the business makes neither a profit nor a loss.">break-even quantity is that minimum level. Sell one unit above it and the business earns profit; sell one unit below and it makes a loss. Knowing the break-even quantity helps entrepreneurs set realistic sales targets, choose an appropriate selling price, and decide whether a business idea is financially viable before committing time and money to it.

You do not need to memorise the break-even formula — it will be given to you in any question that asks you to apply it. The formula is:

Break-even quantity = Fixed costs ÷ (Selling price − Variable cost per unit)

The bracket part — selling price minus variable cost per unit — tells you how much money each sale contributes towards covering the fixed costs. Once enough units have been sold to cover all the fixed costs, the business has broken even.

Key Fact

The break-even formula is: Fixed costs ÷ (Selling price − Variable cost per unit). You will be given this formula in questions that test it — the skill assessed is applying it correctly, not recalling it from memory. Always show your substitution and working clearly.

Worked Calculation

Ferndale Soap Works is a small partnership in Swansea making artisan soaps. Each bar sells at £7.00. Variable costs (ingredients and wrapping) are £2.50 per bar. Monthly fixed costs (rent, insurance, loan interest) total £2,025.

Step 1 — bracket: £7.00 − £2.50 = £4.50 per bar
Step 2 — break-even: £2,025 ÷ £4.50 = 450 bars per month

Ferndale must sell 450 bars every month to cover all its costs. Below 450 it makes a loss; above 450 it makes a profit.

Reading a Break-Even Graph

A break-even graph has output (units) on the horizontal axis and money (£) on the vertical axis. It contains three lines:

  • Fixed costs — a horizontal line starting at the fixed cost level on the vertical axis. It is flat because fixed costs do not change with output.
  • Total costs — a line that starts at the fixed costs level and slopes upward as variable costs are added for each unit produced.
  • Total revenue — a line that starts at zero (no sales = no revenue) and rises with each unit sold.

Where the total revenue line crosses the total costs line is the break-even point. Reading across to the horizontal axis gives you the break-even quantity. Reading up to the vertical axis at that quantity shows that revenue and costs are equal at that point.

Key Fact

To the left of the break-even point on the graph: the loss zone — total costs exceed total revenue. To the right: the profit zone — total revenue exceeds total costs. The vertical gap between the two lines at any given output shows either the profit or the loss at that level of sales.

When costs or the selling price change, the graph shifts in predictable ways — and the formula shows you what happens before you even draw anything:

  • Selling price rises: the revenue line becomes steeper. It crosses the total costs line sooner, so the break-even quantity falls — the business needs to sell fewer units to cover its costs.
  • Fixed costs rise: the total costs line shifts upward (higher starting point). The revenue line does not change, so the break-even quantity rises — more units must be sold to cover the higher fixed costs.
  • Variable cost per unit rises: the total costs line becomes steeper. Again, the break-even quantity rises — each unit contributes less towards fixed costs, so more units are needed.

Using Break-Even to Support Decisions

Break-even analysis is a planning tool. It cannot guarantee success, but it gives a start-up a clear target: “we must sell at least X units per month to avoid a loss.” Before launching, an entrepreneur can use the break-even quantity to ask: “Is this sales target realistic given our market?” If the break-even quantity seems unreachable, the business can adjust — perhaps by cutting fixed costs, finding cheaper materials, or raising the selling price.

The break-even formula assumes that the selling price stays constant for every unit, that variable cost per unit does not change, and that every unit produced is sold. In reality, businesses often offer discounts, face rising material costs, or build up unsold stock. These real-world complications mean that break-even analysis is a useful guide rather than an exact forecast.

Cash vs Profit

Many students assume that a profitable business is automatically in a strong financial position. This is a dangerous misconception. Cash and profit are not the same thing.

Consider a small furniture-maker who sells a £2,000 dining table but agrees to let the customer pay in 60 days. The sale appears in the accounts as £2,000 of revenue — contributing to profit — but the business has received no cash yet. Meanwhile, the business still needs to pay its suppliers this week for the wood, and its staff tomorrow for their wages. If those immediate payments cannot be met, the business may fail even though it is “profitable on paper.”

A start-up can run out of cash for several reasons even when trading profitably:

  • Customers paying late — revenue is counted but cash has not arrived.
  • Paying suppliers upfront — the business spends cash before it has sold the goods made from those supplies.
  • High stock levels — cash is tied up in unsold inventory instead of sitting in the bank.
  • Seasonal demand — sales fall sharply in quiet months but fixed costs continue every month regardless.
exam_tip_html: On break-even calculation questions, the formula will be given to you — so the marks go to correct substitution and a clearly labelled final answer. The most common error is subtracting variable cost from fixed costs (reversing the formula) or forgetting to show the bracket step. Always write the bracket calculation first: selling price minus variable cost per unit, then divide fixed costs by that result. On graph-interpretation questions, read axes carefully before answering — a common mistake is reading the wrong axis or confusing total costs with total revenue. For “explain the difference between cash and profit” questions, link your explanation to a real consequence: it is not enough to say they are different — you must explain that a business can run out of cash even when it is profitable, because customers may pay late while the business still has immediate bills to pay. The “because/therefore/this means that” chain is what moves an answer up the mark bands.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Break-even quantity = Fixed costs ÷ (Selling price − Variable cost per unit). This formula is given in questions; the skill is applying and rearranging it correctly. On a graph, break-even is where the total revenue line crosses the total costs line.
  • If selling price rises, the break-even quantity falls. If fixed or variable costs rise, the break-even quantity rises. These effects can be read from a graph or calculated with the formula.
  • Cash and profit are different. A business can be profitable on paper but still run out of cash if customers pay late, suppliers require upfront payment, or stock builds up unsold. Running out of cash — not lack of profit — is the most common reason new businesses fail.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following statements best describes the break-even quantity?
A) The number of units a business sells in its first month of trading
B) The level of output at which total revenue equals total costs
C) The point at which the business starts to make a profit above its target
D) The maximum number of units a business can produce
practice_questions.marks: B) The level of output at which total revenue equals total costs [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Pebble & Thread is a start-up making handmade greetings cards in Edinburgh. Fixed costs are £900 per month. Each card sells at £6.00. Variable cost per card is £1.50.

Using the formula below, calculate the break-even quantity for Pebble & Thread.

Break-even quantity = Fixed costs ÷ (Selling price − Variable cost per unit)
practice_questions.marks:
Bracket: £6.00 − £1.50 = £4.50
Break-even quantity: £900 ÷ £4.50 = 200 cards per month
[2 marks for correct final answer of 200 cards; 1 mark if bracket is correct (£4.50) but final answer is wrong due to arithmetic error.]

practice_questions.text:
Mossvale Ceramics is a small Ltd company making decorative tiles. Fixed costs are £2,700 per month. Each tile sells at £15.00 and variable costs are £6.00 per tile. Mossvale currently sells 350 tiles per month.

Using the formula below, calculate the break-even quantity and identify whether Mossvale is currently in the profit zone or the loss zone.

Break-even quantity = Fixed costs ÷ (Selling price − Variable cost per unit)
practice_questions.marks:
Bracket: £15.00 − £6.00 = £9.00
Break-even quantity: £2,700 ÷ £9.00 = 300 tiles per month
Mossvale sells 350 tiles, which is above 300, so it is in the profit zone.
[3 marks: 1 mark for correct bracket (£9.00); 1 mark for correct break-even quantity (300); 1 mark for correctly identifying profit zone with reference to actual vs break-even output. Allow follow-through on arithmetic errors.]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which a profitable business might still experience cash problems.
practice_questions.marks: A profitable business may face cash problems if its customers are allowed to delay payment. For example, if a business sells goods worth £3,000 but agrees that the customer has 60 days to pay, the £3,000 is counted as revenue (and contributes to profit), but no cash has actually arrived. This means the business must still pay its own suppliers and wages out of existing cash reserves — and if those reserves are insufficient, the business may be unable to meet its immediate financial obligations even though it is profitable on paper. [1 mark for identifying a relevant cause such as late payment, paying suppliers upfront, or high stock levels; 1 mark for explaining the mechanism (revenue recorded but cash not received); 1 mark for a developed consequence showing how this threatens the business.]

practice_questions.text:
Ridgewick Candles is a sole trader in York. She currently sells 500 candles per month at £8.00 each. Variable costs are £3.00 per candle. Monthly fixed costs are £1,750.

Her landlord has told her that rent will rise by £350 per month from next month. Her selling price and variable costs will stay the same.

Analyse how the rent increase will affect Ridgewick Candles' financial position.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Calculates or clearly explains the impact on break-even quantity (new fixed costs = £2,100; bracket = £5.00; new break-even = 420 candles, up from original 350 candles at £1,750 ÷ £5.00). Demonstrates the impact on profit (profit falls from [500×£5 = £2,500 revenue less costs of £1,750 + 500×£3] to new profit with higher fixed costs). Shows awareness that if actual sales remain at 500, the business is still above break-even but with a smaller profit, and analyses the risk if sales were to fall. Conclusion is grounded in the specific scenario.

Secure (3–4 marks): Correctly identifies that higher fixed costs raise the break-even quantity and reduce profit. Uses some specific figures from the scenario. Development is present but may not fully analyse the impact on the profit zone.

Developing (2 marks): Identifies that more units must be sold or that profit will fall, without quantitative support or developed reasoning.

Emerging (1 mark): States that costs will rise with minimal development.

practice_questions.text:
'A business that is making a profit does not need to worry about running out of cash.'

Discuss whether you agree with this statement. Use the example of Copperoak Furniture, a small sole trader in Bristol that sells bespoke oak dining sets at £1,800 each, with customers paying 90 days after delivery.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Develops a clear and balanced argument. Explains convincingly why profit and cash are different concepts using the scenario (revenue counted at point of sale; cash arrives 90 days later; meanwhile wages, materials and fixed costs must be paid from existing funds). Identifies specific causes of cash problems (late payment, paying suppliers upfront, high stock tied up in bespoke orders). Reaches a well-supported conclusion that the statement is largely incorrect, with a nuanced point — for example, that a highly profitable business with adequate reserves may be resilient enough to manage the 90-day gap, but a start-up with limited reserves is at significant risk.

Secure (5–7 marks): Clearly explains the cash-vs-profit distinction with reference to the scenario. Develops both sides (why profit matters; why cash is still at risk) with some development. Conclusion is present.

Developing (3–4 marks): Identifies that cash and profit are different and gives one reason why a profitable business might still run out of cash. Limited use of the scenario detail.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Agrees or disagrees with the statement with minimal justification. Little or no use of the scenario.

knowledge_checks.q: On a break-even graph, what does the area to the right of the break-even point represent?
options: The loss zone, where costs exceed revenue
The profit zone, where revenue exceeds costs
The fixed cost zone, where no variable costs apply
The break-even zone, where profit equals zero

knowledge_checks.q: If a business raises its selling price per unit (and everything else stays the same), what happens to the break-even quantity?
options: It rises — more units are needed to cover costs
It falls — fewer units are needed to cover costs
It stays the same — price does not affect break-even
It doubles — because revenue has increased

knowledge_checks.q: Break-even quantity = Fixed costs ÷ (Selling price − _____ per unit).
On a break-even graph, the total revenue line starts at _____ because there is no revenue when no units are sold.
Match each change to its effect on the break-even quantity:
right: Break-even quantity falls — each sale covers fixed costs faster
Break-even quantity rises — the starting point of total costs is higher
Break-even quantity rises — each sale covers less of the fixed costs

flashcard_questions.a: The level of output at which total revenue equals total costs — no profit, no loss.

flashcard_questions.q: Do you need to recall the break-even formula in the written exam?
flashcard_questions.a: No — the formula is given; the skill tested is applying it correctly.

flashcard_questions.q: Formula cloze: Break-even quantity = Fixed costs ÷ (Selling price − _____).
On a break-even graph, where is the break-even point?
flashcard_questions.a: Where the total revenue line crosses the total costs line.

flashcard_questions.q: If fixed costs rise, what happens to the break-even quantity?
flashcard_questions.a: It rises — more units must be sold to cover the higher fixed costs.

flashcard_questions.q: If the selling price per unit rises, what happens to the break-even quantity?
flashcard_questions.a: It falls — each sale contributes more towards fixed costs.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the area to the left of the break-even point on the graph represent?
flashcard_questions.a: The loss zone — total costs exceed total revenue.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between cash and profit?
flashcard_questions.a: Profit is revenue minus total costs; cash is money actually available in the business right now.

flashcard_questions.q: Why can a profitable business still run out of cash?
flashcard_questions.a: Customers may pay late, so revenue is counted before cash is received.

flashcard_questions.q: Give two causes of cash problems for a start-up.
flashcard_questions.a: Late customer payments, paying suppliers upfront (also accept: high stock levels, seasonal demand).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the most common reason new businesses fail — lack of profit or lack of cash?
flashcard_questions.a: Lack of cash — they may be profitable on paper but unable to pay immediate bills.

glossary_terms.definition: The quantity of output at which total revenue exactly equals total costs; the business makes neither a profit nor a loss.
The actual money available in a business's bank account or till at any given moment, used to pay immediate expenses.
The area on a break-even graph to the right of the break-even point, where total revenue exceeds total costs.
The area on a break-even graph to the left of the break-even point, where total costs exceed total revenue.
The total money a business takes from selling its products before any costs are subtracted.
